title: Speech and language development disorders in children
intro: Children learn to speak at different speeds, but some have lasting difficulties understanding or using language or producing speech sounds. Early help improves communication, learning and confidence. If you are worried, do not simply wait, since assessment and speech therapy can start early.

sections.heading: Typical development
paragraphs: Most children say first words around the first birthday, combine two words around the age of two, and speak in short sentences by three, with strangers understanding much of what they say by about three to four years. Understanding comes before speaking. Some children are late talkers who catch up, but others do not.

sections.heading: Types of difficulties
paragraphs: Language disorders affect understanding or using words and grammar. Speech sound disorders affect pronunciation. Stuttering involves disrupted fluency, and voice disorders affect the quality of the voice. Causes include hearing loss, developmental delay, autism, neurological conditions, family history, or no known cause. Growing up with two languages does not cause delay.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: Seek advice if a child does not babble by one year, has no words by about eighteen months, does not combine words by two, is hard to understand at three, does not seem to understand simple instructions, loses skills, or avoids speaking. Parents' instinct that something is wrong should be taken seriously.

sections.heading: Assessment
paragraphs: A hearing test is always an important first step. A paediatrician and speech and language therapist assess understanding, expression, speech sounds and play. They may involve psychologists or specialists when other developmental areas are affected.

sections.heading: Therapy and support
paragraphs: Speech and language therapy uses play-based exercises tailored to the child, with parents learning how to support at home. Talk with your child, read aloud, sing, describe activities, give time to respond and repeat words correctly without correcting harshly. Nursery or school support helps. Many children make good progress, though some need long-term help.

examples.title: Raising concern
examples.text: Imagine your two-year-old uses only a few words. You could ask your paediatrician for a hearing test and speech therapy assessment, and note which words your child understands.

examples.title: Practising at home
examples.text: Suppose your therapist suggests practice at home. You might include short daily sessions during play, reading or bath time without pressure.
